answer: No, they do not behave the same. Using only pre-fire features, among inspected structures (excl. uninspected/inaccessible), the feature-outcome relationships differ materially. Palisades: more neighbors (AUC 0.72) and tighter spacing (0.66) track destruction, slope weakly (0.55). Eaton: neighbors/spacing carry no signal (0.48/0.48), slope is modestly informative (0.62). Open-land distance has the opposite sign to the pre-set 'nearer open land is riskier' direction in both fires (destroyed structures were farther from open land; AUC 0.32 Eaton, 0.41 Palisades), much more strongly in Eaton. Only slope agrees in sign and rough size (adj. odds ratio per SD 1.15 vs 1.12). A model fit on one fire does not transfer (AUC 0.50 and 0.48 vs 0.71/0.74 in-fire). Association only, not causal; wind/embers/vegetation/hardening not in data.
traps_or_caveats: Uninspected footprints (no DINS record: 11,770 Eaton, 3,223 Palisades) excluded, not treated as survivors; 41 Eaton 'Inaccessible' also excluded. Eaton has far lower inspection coverage (~61% vs ~79%), so selection into the inspected sample may differ between fires.
Layer was selected by the final fire perimeters (1/4 mile buffer), so this describes structures the fire reached, not where fire will spread; perimeter distance was not used as a predictor.

Open-land distance is built from the same perimeter-selected layer (open land only counted >400 m inside the hull), so it partly encodes position within the burned footprint/edge effect; its reversed sign should not be read as 'open land is protective'. Fixed a-priori direction is contradicted in both fires.

Features are strongly correlated (density, spacing, open-land distance), so the multivariable coefficients, including the sign flip of neighbors_50m in Eaton (OR 0.65 vs Palisades 2.69), are conditional effects and unstable to interpret; univariate AUCs are the cleaner comparison.

Fire assigned by footprint centroid easting (<380000 m UTM 11N = Palisades), as in the case code; 3DEP slope at 5 m is coarse relative to a house; 'destroyed' = DINS >50%, severity is inspector-judged.

Spatial autocorrelation: neighboring houses burn together, so bootstrap CIs (iid resampling, 200 reps) are far too narrow; the differences between fires are large enough that the conclusion holds, but p-values/CIs are optimistic.

Not available/not estimated: wind, embers, vegetation, roof material, defensible space, firefighting response; these likely differ between the two wind-driven fires and explain much of the difference. No causal claim.
